summary: A 1974 report on a protocol experiment run at BBN, when the TENEX line printer failed and the PDP-11 line printer was used over the ARPANET. It also served to study network protocols, based on the Cerf and Kahn design. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A printer broke, so the team printed on a different machine through the network, and used the chance to test how well the rules for sending worked.

subtitle: A 1974 experiment that sent print jobs across the ARPANET to study an early reliable end-to-end protocol.

tldr.problem: BBN's main line printer failed, and the team wanted to use a PDP-11 printer over the network while also studying network protocols.
tldr.mechanism: They implemented a sliding-window protocol based on Cerf and Kahn's INWG Note #39, with sequence numbers, ACKs, a 10 second timeout, and a "say again" flag.
tldr.outcome: The experiment exposed a problem when the receiver restarts, led to a recommendation of 32-bit sequence numbers, and left several features untested.

today: RFC 700 is an Informational RFC with no replacement listed in its metadata. It reports an experiment from 1974 and recommends, rather than defines, further work.

sections.title: The Experiment
sections.content: In early February 1974 the main line printer on BBN's TENEX system failed. The authors decided to use the PDP-11 line printer via the ARPANET, both to get listings and to study network protocols. The design was based on the protocol described by Cerf and Kahn in INWG Note #39, and not all of its features were implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: When the usual printer broke, the team sent their pages to another printer over the network, and watched how well their sending rules worked.

sections.title: How the Protocol Worked
sections.content:
The sender keeps two pointers into the byte stream: LEFT (everything before it is sent and acknowledged) and RIGHT (the edge of the window of bytes sent but not yet acknowledged). The low order 16 bits of RIGHT travel with each message as a sequence number. The receiver discards messages outside its buffer or with bad checksums, but must still acknowledge messages to the left of LEFT so a lost ACK does not cause endless retransmission.

An ACK names the next byte the receiver wants and its available buffer space. If ACKs stop, a 10 second timeout makes the sender retransmit the whole window. The "Say Again" extension lets the receiver force retransmission of the window with a flag. Two flags set up an association: FRST (like SYN in INWG Note #39) marks the first message, and HUH is the receiver asking the sender to define the sequence numbers.

Messages carried zero to 255 bytes of data and a one-byte checksum. The window was a constant 2048 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps a stack of pages it has not heard back about. The receiver says what it got, and if nothing comes back for a while, the sender sends the stack again.

sections.title: The Restart Problem and Rate Calculations
sections.content:
If the PDP-11 receiver was reloaded while the sender was running, the first few pages printed about six times. The sender had been retransmitting a whole window; the restarted receiver answered each message with HUH, and the sender put FRST on the first message of each of six retransmissions, so the receiver restarted the stream repeatedly. Ignoring messages after an HUH until a FRST arrives is not acceptable in general, since a lost message leaves the port useless.

The authors also derive that, in steady state without errors, bandwidth is B = W/2T, the window divided by the round trip time. With an error fraction of 0.01, W of 20 messages and T of 0.5 second, the 10 second timeout gives 6.7, but forced retransmission gives 20. For rejecting duplicates they recommend a 32-bit sequence number field, assuming a 1 MegaByte per second network and a 500 second message lifetime.
sections.plainLanguage: When the receiver was switched off and on, the sender kept resending, and the pages came out six times. The team also did some math about how fast the sending could go.

sections.title: Untested Features and Proposed Additions
sections.content:
None of the programs supported window size control, reassembly, expanded internetwork addresses, multiple associations or reliable making and breaking of associations. The authors also recommend a more reliable checksum than the one used: the low eight bits of the twos complement negation of the sum of all other bytes.

For refusing a SYN, the RFC proposes releases named REJECT, ABORT and ABNORMAL. During an association, the sender could release with DONE or GAG.
sections.plainLanguage: There were things they did not try yet, and a few ideas for polite ways to say "no thanks" or "I am finished".
